chapter_title: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: Swinging Arcs to Build an Equilateral Triangle

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Construct, section 7.1 p.150
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles with these sidelengths (all in cm) using compass and ruler: (a) 4, 4, 6; (b) 3, 4, 5; (c) 1, 5, 5; (d) 4, 6, 8; (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.150
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use points on a circle and/or its centre to form isosceles triangles (diagram given with one circle).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.1 p.150
homework.description: Use points on two (or three) equal circles and/or their centres A, B (and C) to form isosceles and equilateral triangles.

time_bands.activity: Open by asking students to try drawing an equilateral triangle freehand using a marked ruler. Collect a few attempts and discuss why trial-and-error makes this inefficient. Surface the idea from Grade 6 that arcs can locate a point equidistant from two given points.

Walk through the three-step arc procedure: draw base AB of 4 cm, swing an arc of 4 cm from A, swing a second arc of 4 cm from B, and mark C at the intersection. Students carry out Construct, section 7.1 p.150 ('Construct triangles with these sidelengths (all in cm) using compass and ruler....'), working through at least parts (a), (b), and (e) independently. Circulate and prompt: why must both arcs have the same radius as the base?

Students attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.150 ('Use points on a circle and/or its centre to form isosceles triangles....'). Pairs compare their triangles and articulate why every chord of a circle equals the radius only when the arc-radius equals the circle's radius.

Brief whole-class share: collect one or two constructed triangles under the visualiser. Students state in their own words why C lies on both arcs and therefore AC = BC = AB. Set Figure it Out Q2, section 7.1 p.150 as a quick reinforcement task for home.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who swing arcs of different radii for A and B — this is the most common slip; ask them to measure AC and BC afterwards to self-correct. The arc-intersection reasoning (C lies on both arcs, so both distances equal the radius) is the conceptual load of this unit and should be drawn out explicitly in the share. Students who finish early can explore whether the construction still works when the arc radius is smaller than AB.

textbook_segments.title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given

periods.activity_title: When Do Three Lengths Build a Triangle?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 7.2 p.151
textbook_items_in_class.description: Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm. Find more sets of lengths for which a triangle is impossible, and identify a pattern.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.154
textbook_items_in_class.description: Without constructing: could you have determined that 3, 4, 8 cm and 2, 3, 6 cm cannot form triangles? Explain using the triangle inequality.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.154
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine whether triangles exist for: (a) 10 km, 10 km, 25 km; (b) 5 mm, 10 mm, 20 mm; (c) 12 cm, 20 cm, 40 cm.

homework.description: For any set of three lengths, will at least two comparisons always satisfy 'direct length < sum of other two'? Explore. Also find which length can be identified as immediately less than the sum without calculation.

time_bands.activity: Students attempt to construct triangles with 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm as posed in Math Talk, section 7.2 p.151 ('Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm....'). Students draw and discover that the arcs do not intersect. Prompt: what went wrong geometrically?

Introduce the tent-tree-pole path metaphor: a direct path between two points is always shorter than a route via a third point. Students try to express this for sides a, b, c. Guide the class to articulate the triangle inequality (each side < sum of the other two). Discuss the circle-intersection cases: circles touch, do not intersect, intersect internally — which case corresponds to each failing set?

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.154 ('Without constructing: could you have determined that 3, 4, 8 cm and 2, 3, 6 cm cannot form triangles?...') and Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.154 ('Determine whether triangles exist for: (a) 10 km, 10 km, 25 km; (b) 5 mm, 10 mm, 20 mm; (c) 12 cm, 20 cm, 40 cm.'). Students verify by checking all three inequality comparisons for each set.

Pairs share one case each; class confirms the pattern. Students note in their books: the triangle inequality is both necessary and sufficient for existence. Set Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.154 for home exploration.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often check only one inequality (the longest side vs the sum of the other two) and miss that all three must hold; prompt them to write all three comparisons systematically. The visual of two circles failing to intersect (or merely touching) is powerful — have students sketch the circle diagrams alongside the numerical check. The tent-tree-pole metaphor grounding the reasoning is in the chapter prose and can be read aloud if students are struggling to verbalise why a direct path must be shorter.

textbook_segments.title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given

periods.activity_title: Applying the Inequality: Constructing Valid Triangles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which sets of lengths can be sidelengths of a triangle? Explain: (a) 2, 2, 5; (b) 3, 4, 6; (c) 2, 4, 8; (d) 5, 5, 8; (e) 10, 20, 25; (f) 10, 20, 35; (g) 24, 26, 28.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 7.2 p.158
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find 3 examples each of sidelength sets where the two circles: (a) touch each other at a point; (b) do not intersect. Frame a complete procedure to check the existence of a triangle.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.159
textbook_items_in_class.description: Check if a triangle exists for: (a) 1, 100, 100; (b) 3, 6, 9; (c) 1, 1, 5; (d) 5, 10, 12.

homework.description: For each pair of given sides, find at least 5 valid values for the third side: (a) 1, 100; (b) 5, 5; (c) 3, 7. Describe all possible third-side values for each case.

time_bands.activity: Students work independently on Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156 ('Which sets of lengths can be sidelengths of a triangle? Explain: (a) 2, 2, 5; (b) 3, 4, 6....'), applying the triangle inequality systematically and writing a one-line justification for each case. Circulate and look for students checking all three comparisons.

Students explore Figure it Out, section 7.2 p.158 ('Find 3 examples each of sidelength sets where the two circles: (a) touch each other at a point; (b) do not intersect....'), constructing or sketching the circle diagrams and then drafting a complete procedure for checking triangle existence. Groups share their written procedures and the class converges on a canonical three-step check.

Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.159 ('Check if a triangle exists for: (a) 1, 100, 100; (b) 3, 6, 9; (c) 1, 1, 5; (d) 5, 10, 12.'), using the procedure agreed upon. They also discuss Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.159 ('Does an equilateral triangle exist with sides 50, 50, 50?...') orally.

Quick pair-check: each student poses one new set of three lengths to their partner and challenges them to decide existence without a ruler. Set Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.159 to find the full range of valid third-side values for given pairs.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established the triangle inequality as both necessary and sufficient, this unit builds fluency in applying it. The most productive error to watch for is treating the check as a single comparison (longest side vs sum) rather than a three-way check; Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156 part (g) — 24, 26, 28 — passes all three and is a good counter-example to the shortcut. The circle-diagram framing from the previous unit helps students see why the degenerate (touching) case fails: a 'triangle' of zero area is not a triangle.

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

periods.activity_title: Two Sides, One Angle — Discovering When a Triangle Exists

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles given two sides and the included angle: (a) 3 cm, 75°, 7 cm; (b) 6 cm, 25°, 3 cm; (c) 3 cm, 120°, 8 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 7.3 p.161
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is there a combination of two sides and an included angle for which a triangle is not possible? Justify from your construction observations.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 7.3 p.162
textbook_items_in_class.description: Do triangles always exist for every combination of two angles and the included side? Find examples where they do not.

time_bands.activity: Pose the question: if you know two sides and the angle between them, can you always build a triangle? Students predict yes or no and give a quick reason to a partner.

Students carry out Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161 ('Construct triangles given two sides and the included angle: (a) 3 cm, 75°, 7 cm; (b) 6 cm, 25°, 3 cm; (c) 3 cm, 120°, 8 cm.'), using the four-step SAS construction: draw base, construct the given angle at one endpoint, mark the second side length on the angle arm, and join to close. Students compare their finished triangles.

Students tackle Math Talk, section 7.3 p.161 ('Is there a combination of two sides and an included angle for which a triangle is not possible?...') — they try extreme angles (approaching 180° or beyond) and sketch what happens. The class discusses: when the included angle is ≥ 180° the construction breaks down.

Pivot to two angles and an included side. Students attempt Math Talk, section 7.3 p.162 ('Do triangles always exist for every combination of two angles and the included side?...'), discovering that when two base angles sum to 180° the arms are parallel and never meet. Students write a conjecture in their own words about when this construction fails.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often forget to place the protractor origin at the base endpoint when constructing the angle arm — circulate and check instrument placement early. The key reasoning discovery is that an included angle ≥ 180° cannot produce a closed triangle; let students articulate this themselves from their sketches before confirming. The two-angles case failure (sum ≥ 180°) foreshadows the angle-sum property that follows in this section.

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

periods.activity_title: Parallel-Line Proof of the Angle Sum Property

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 7.3 p.164
textbook_items_in_class.description: Experiment with different triangles to find a relation between any two angles and the third. What data will you track and how will you organise it?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.165
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the third angle (using a parallel-line argument) when two angles are: (a) 36°, 72°; (b) 150°, 15°; (c) 90°, 30°; (d) 75°, 45°.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.165
textbook_items_in_class.description: Can a triangle have all three angles equal to 70°? If two angles are 70°, what is the third? If all angles are equal, what must each be?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Try This Q3, section 7.3 p.165
textbook_items_in_class.description: In triangle ABC, ∠B = ∠C and ∠A = 50°. Find ∠B and ∠C.

time_bands.activity: Students measure all three angles of three different hand-drawn triangles and record the sums, as prompted by Math Talk, section 7.3 p.164 ('Experiment with different triangles to find a relation between any two angles and the third....') They notice the sum is always close to 180° and state a conjecture.

Present the parallel-line proof formally: draw XY ∥ BC through vertex A; identify ∠XAB = ∠B as alternate interior angles; identify ∠YAC = ∠C as alternate interior angles; note that ∠XAB + ∠BAC + ∠YAC forms a straight angle at A, giving ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°. Students copy and annotate the proof in their books, supplying the reason for each step.

Students apply the property in Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.165 ('Find the third angle (using a parallel-line argument) when two angles are: (a) 36°, 72°; (b) 150°, 15°; (c) 90°, 30°; (d) 75°, 45°.') and Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.165 ('Can a triangle have all three angles equal to 70°?...'). They also solve Try This Q3, section 7.3 p.165 ('In triangle ABC, ∠B = ∠C and ∠A = 50°. Find ∠B and ∠C.').

Whole-class: students explain part (b) of Figure it Out Q1 (150° + 15° = 165°, so third angle = 15°, valid) in their own words. Confirm: the angle-sum property constrains every triangle's angles simultaneously.

periods.teacher_notes: The most frequent error is stating alternate angles without naming the parallel line — insist that students write 'alternate interior angles, XY ∥ BC' as the explicit reason. Part (b) of Figure it Out Q1 surprises many students (a 150° angle in a triangle is obtuse but still valid if the other two are small enough); use it to reinforce that the property is about the sum, not any individual angle. Students who finish early can explore: if ∠A = 2∠B = 4∠C, what are the angles?

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

periods.activity_title: ASA Constructions and the Exterior Angle

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.162
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles given two angles and the included side: (a) 75°, 5 cm, 75°; (b) 25°, 3 cm, 60°; (c) 120°, 6 cm, 30°.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.163
textbook_items_in_class.description: For each given angle (a) 30°; (b) 70°; (c) 54°; (d) 144°, find at least two angles for which a triangle is possible and two for which it is not. Find the third angle in each valid case.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.163
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine which angle pairs can be two angles of a triangle: (a) 35°, 150°; (b) 70°, 30°; (c) 90°, 85°; (d) 50°, 150°.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 7.3 p.166
textbook_items_in_class.description: Exterior angle: find ∠ACD if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°. Then find the exterior angle for different ∠A and ∠B values and derive the relationship between the exterior angle and the two non-adjacent interior angles.

time_bands.activity: Students construct the triangles in Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.162 ('Construct triangles given two angles and the included side: (a) 75°, 5 cm, 75°; (b) 25°, 3 cm, 60°; (c) 120°, 6 cm, 30°.') — draw base, construct angles at both endpoints, and find C as the intersection of the two arms. For (c), students discover that 120° + 30° = 150° < 180°, so C exists; they check this with the angle-sum property established earlier.

Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.163 ('For each given angle (a) 30°; (b) 70°; (c) 54°; (d) 144°, find at least two angles for which a triangle is possible....') and Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.163 ('Determine which angle pairs can be two angles of a triangle....'), applying ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180° as a decision rule and computing valid third angles.

Introduce the exterior angle: using Figure it Out, section 7.3 p.166 ('Exterior angle: find ∠ACD if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°....'), students compute ∠ACD = 110°, then tabulate results for several ∠A, ∠B values and derive the exterior-angle theorem: exterior angle = sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles.
Students state the exterior-angle theorem in one sentence in their own words and write one numerical check to verify their statement.

periods.teacher_notes: A common slip in ASA construction is drawing both angle arms from the same endpoint; ensure students construct one angle at each end of the base. The exterior-angle theorem emerges naturally from the angle-sum property (exterior angle + interior angle at C = 180°, and interior angle at C = 180° − ∠A − ∠B, so exterior = ∠A + ∠B) — prompt students to derive it symbolically rather than just observing it numerically. Students who see that (c) of Figure it Out Q1 p.162 has a 150° interior angle will need reassurance that the angle-sum condition, not the size of any single angle, is the existence test.

textbook_segments.title: Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles

periods.activity_title: Finding the Height: Set-Square and Paper-Fold Altitudes

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.168
textbook_items_in_class.description: Visualise and draw a rough diagram: in what type of triangle is a side also an altitude?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity, section 7.4 p.168
textbook_items_in_class.description: Altitudes Using Paper Folding: cut out a paper triangle, fix one side as the base, and fold so the crease is the altitude from the top vertex to the base. Justify why the crease is perpendicular to the base.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.169
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct the altitude from A to BC using ruler and set square, for the given triangle (extended base case shown also).

time_bands.activity: Pose the visualisation in Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.168 ('Visualise and draw a rough diagram: in what type of triangle is a side also an altitude?'). Students sketch their diagrams; class converges on: in a right-angled triangle, either leg is the altitude to the other leg. Introduce the definition: the altitude from vertex A is the perpendicular segment from A to line BC.

Students carry out Activity, section 7.4 p.168 ('Altitudes Using Paper Folding: cut out a paper triangle, fix one side as the base, and fold so the crease is the altitude from the top vertex to the base. Justify why the crease is perpendicular to the base.'). They fold and crease, then place a set-square against the crease and base to verify the 90° angle. Students articulate why the fold creates a perpendicular.

Students work on Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.169 ('Construct the altitude from A to BC using ruler and set square, for the given triangle (extended base case shown also).'), using the set-square-and-ruler method: align ruler to base, place set square on ruler, slide until the vertical edge meets vertex A, draw the altitude. Students also attempt the extended-base case where the foot of the altitude falls outside the triangle.

Quick share: one student demonstrates the extended-base construction under the visualiser. Class notes when the altitude foot falls outside the triangle and discusses which triangle types produce this situation.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error is placing the set square so that its vertical edge does not pass through the vertex — have students mark the vertex with a dot and check alignment before drawing. The paper-folding activity is the hands-on verification that the crease is perpendicular, and students should be pressed to explain why folding one layer onto itself makes the two half-lines coincide and therefore creates a 90° angle. The extended-base case (altitude foot outside the triangle) is new for many students; emphasise that the definition refers to the line through BC, not the segment.

periods.activity_title: Classifying Triangles: Sides, Angles, and Their Interplay

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct the altitude from A to BC.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangle TRY with RY = 4 cm, TR = 7 cm, ∠R = 140°. Construct the altitude from T to RY.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Through construction, explore whether it is possible to construct: (a) a right-angled equilateral triangle; (b) an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle; (c) a right-angled isosceles triangle; (d) an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the two classification systems — by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and by angles (acute-angled, right-angled, obtuse-angled) — through a sorting task: display six triangle sketches and students place each in a two-way grid (sides × angles). Elicit that an equilateral triangle is always acute-angled.

Students construct Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.170 ('Construct triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct the altitude from A to BC.') and Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.170 ('Construct triangle TRY with RY = 4 cm, TR = 7 cm, ∠R = 140°. Construct the altitude from T to RY.'). They identify each triangle's type by both sides and angles after constructing.

Students explore Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170 ('Through construction, explore whether it is possible to construct: (a) a right-angled equilateral triangle; (b) an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle; (c) a right-angled isosceles triangle; (d) an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.'), constructing or attempting to construct each combination and using the angle-sum property to justify why (a) and (b) are impossible.

Class shares findings from Figure it Out Q4. Students state the rule: equilateral ⟹ all angles 60° ⟹ always acute; right-angled isosceles and obtuse-angled isosceles are both possible. Students annotate their two-way grid accordingly.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes think a triangle can be both equilateral and right-angled; Figure it Out Q4 parts (a) and (b) are designed to settle this via the angle-sum constraint (three equal angles must each be 60°). For Figure it Out Q2, the 140° obtuse angle means the altitude from T falls outside the triangle — connect this to the extended-base altitude case covered when constructing altitudes. The two-way grid is a useful organiser to keep on the board throughout this unit.

periods.activity_title: Right-Angled Triangles, Hypotenuse, and Shortest Paths

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Try This Q3, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct right-angled triangle ∆ABC with ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm. How many different triangles exist with these measurements? (Note: other measurements can take any values.)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 7.5 p.172
textbook_items_in_class.description: Shortest Path in a Box: a spider at one corner of a box wants to walk (on the surfaces) to the opposite corner. Mark the shortest path on a cardboard box and compare with classmates. (Hint diagram shows unfolded surfaces.)

time_bands.activity: Students attempt Try This Q3, section 7.5 p.170 ('Construct right-angled triangle ∆ABC with ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm. How many different triangles exist with these measurements?'). They draw multiple triangles with different AB and BC values but the same ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm, and discuss how many essentially different triangles are possible.

Brief consolidation: students compile a personal reference card listing the six triangle types (equilateral, isosceles, scalene; acute-angled, right-angled, obtuse-angled) with a sketch and one defining property for each. They also note the key inter-relationships discovered through construction.

Students engage with Figure it Out, section 7.5 p.172 ('Shortest Path in a Box: a spider at one corner of a box wants to walk (on the surfaces) to the opposite corner. Mark the shortest path on a cardboard box and compare with classmates.'). Students cut and unfold a cardboard box (or use a paper net), mark candidate paths, and measure to find the shortest. Groups compare answers and discuss why unfolding transforms a surface-path problem into a straight-line (triangle) problem.

Quick whole-class discussion: how does the shortest-path problem connect to the triangle inequality established when studying three given sides? Students articulate the link between a straight line being the shortest path and the triangle inequality.

periods.teacher_notes: Try This Q3 is intentionally open-ended: with only ∠B = 90° and AC fixed, the third side AB can take any value in (0, 5), producing infinitely many distinct right-angled triangles. Students who claim only one triangle exists are likely fixing AB unconsciously; invite them to vary AB and recheck. The box puzzle is a rich spatial-reasoning task — encourage students to consider at least two different unfolding routes and measure both before concluding; the 'obvious' unfolding is rarely the shortest path.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct the altitude from A to BC.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangle TRY with RY = 4 cm, TR = 7 cm, ∠R = 140°. Construct the altitude from T to RY.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Through construction, explore whether it is possible to construct: (a) a right-angled equilateral triangle; (b) an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle; (c) a right-angled isosceles triangle; (d) an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.

time_bands.activity: Students who have not yet fully completed Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.170 ('Construct triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct the altitude from A to BC.') and Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.170 ('Construct triangle TRY with RY = 4 cm, TR = 7 cm, ∠R = 140°. Construct the altitude from T to RY.') do so now, while others extend by measuring all angles and confirming the triangle type by both classifications.

Class revisits Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170 ('Through construction, explore whether it is possible to construct: (a) a right-angled equilateral triangle; (b) an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle; (c) a right-angled isosceles triangle; (d) an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.') — students who attempted this earlier now write formal justifications using the angle-sum property (∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°) for parts (a) and (b), and produce a completed construction for (c) and (d).

Students design their own challenge: given only the angle classification (acute/right/obtuse), they choose side lengths that produce a triangle of that type, construct it, measure the angles to verify, and then classify it by sides as well. Partners swap and verify each other's constructions.

Brief oral round: each student names one impossible type combination (e.g., right-angled equilateral) and gives a one-sentence reason using the angle-sum property. This closes the classification work on firm conceptual ground.

periods.teacher_notes: The angle-sum argument that rules out right-angled and obtuse-angled equilateral triangles (three equal angles must each be 60°, leaving no room for a 90° or obtuse angle) is the key conceptual closure for the classification strand. Watch for students who attempt to justify impossibility by appeal to construction difficulty alone; insist on the algebraic argument. The student-design task in the third band is deliberately open so that confident students can explore more unusual combinations (e.g., acute-angled scalene) while others consolidate the standard types.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly states all six types of triangles covered in the classification of triangles by sides and by angles?

options.label: A
options.text: Equilateral, isosceles, scalene; acute-angled, reflex-angled, obtuse-angled

options.label: B
options.text: Equilateral, isosceles, scalene; acute-angled, right-angled, obtuse-angled

options.label: C
options.text: Equilateral, isosceles, scalene; acute-angled, right-angled, straight-angled

options.label: D
options.text: Equilateral, right-angled, scalene; acute-angled, isosceles, obtuse-angled

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A — Equilateral, isosceles, scalene (by sides); acute-angled, right-angled, obtuse-angled (by angles).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the two independent classification systems stated in section 7.5: three side-based types and three angle-based types.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has confused 'right-angled' with 'reflex-angled'; reflex angles (> 180°) cannot appear as interior angles of a triangle.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has mixed up the two classification systems, placing an angle-based type (right-angled) in the side-based list and a side-based type (isosceles) in the angle-based list.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has replaced 'obtuse-angled' with 'straight-angled'; a straight angle (180°) cannot be an interior angle of a triangle because the angle sum would be exceeded.

inclusivity.support: Look back at the sorted triangle sketches and the two-way classification grid from the lesson.
inclusivity.challenge: Give one example of a triangle type that appears in both systems simultaneously and explain why.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.170
exercise.description: Construct triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct the altitude from A to BC.

items.prompt: A triangle has one angle equal to 140°. Which of the following correctly classifies this triangle by its angles?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — A triangle with one angle greater than 90° is an obtuse-angled triangle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the angle-based classification: one obtuse interior angle (> 90°) makes the triangle obtuse-angled.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has confused the classification; an acute-angled triangle requires all three angles to be less than 90°.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused obtuse with right; a right-angled triangle has exactly one 90° angle, not a 140° angle.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused angle-based classification with side-based classification; equilateral is a side-based type and requires all angles to be 60°.

inclusivity.support: Review the definition: a triangle is obtuse-angled if one interior angle is greater than 90°.
inclusivity.challenge: If one angle is 140°, what is the largest the other two angles can each be, and what does that tell you about the triangle's shape?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.170
exercise.description: Construct triangle TRY with RY = 4 cm, TR = 7 cm, ∠R = 140°. Construct the altitude from T to RY.

items.prompt: Which of the following triangle type combinations is impossible?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: D — A right-angled equilateral triangle is impossible because an equilateral triangle has all angles equal to 60°, and 60° ≠ 90°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the angle-sum property: three equal angles must each be 60°, so no interior angle can be 90°.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student incorrectly excluded a valid combination; a right-angled isosceles triangle (e.g., 90°, 45°, 45°) is constructible.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student incorrectly excluded a valid combination; an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle (e.g., 120°, 30°, 30°) is constructible.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student incorrectly excluded a valid combination; an acute-angled scalene triangle (e.g., 50°, 60°, 70° with all sides different) is constructible.

inclusivity.support: Use the angle-sum property: for an equilateral triangle, what must each angle equal?
inclusivity.challenge: Name one more impossible combination (other than obtuse-angled equilateral) and write a one-sentence justification using the angle-sum property.

items.section_title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given
items.prompt: Priya says that the three lengths 6 cm, 6 cm, and 13 cm can form a triangle because two of the sides are equal. Is Priya correct? Justify your answer using the triangle inequality.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Priya is incorrect. The triangle inequality requires each side to be less than the sum of the other two. Here: 6 + 6 = 12, which is less than 13, so the longest side (13 cm) is not less than the sum of the other two (12 cm). Therefore no triangle can be formed with these lengths.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check all three triangle-inequality comparisons; the critical one here is 6 + 6 = 12 < 13, which fails.

inclusivity.support: Try to construct the triangle with a compass and see whether the two arcs of radius 6 cm actually meet.
inclusivity.challenge: Find the largest integer value of the third side that would make a triangle with the two 6 cm sides valid, and explain why your chosen value works.

exercise.description: Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm. Find more sets of lengths for which a triangle is impossible, and identify a pattern.

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: In triangle PQR, the angle at Q is the included angle between sides PQ and QR. A student sets the included angle to 185°. Explain, with a reason, why no triangle can be formed in this situation.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: An included angle of 185° is greater than 180°. When the angle arm at Q is rotated 185° from the base, the arm points away from the other base endpoint rather than towards it, so the two sides PQ and QR open beyond a straight line and the third vertex never closes the triangle. Moreover, a single interior angle ≥ 180° would make the angle sum exceed 180°, violating the angle-sum property for triangles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: An interior angle must be strictly between 0° and 180°; an angle ≥ 180° makes the two sides diverge and prevents closure.

inclusivity.support: Sketch what happens when the angle arm swings past a straight angle — does the arm ever point back to close the triangle?
inclusivity.challenge: If the included angle were exactly 180°, what shape would PQ and QR form together, and why is that still not a triangle?

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: In triangle ABC, a line XY is drawn through A parallel to BC. The angles ∠XAB and ∠YAC are marked. Explain, step by step, how this construction proves that ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Step 1: Since XY ∥ BC, angles ∠XAB and ∠ABC are alternate interior angles, so ∠XAB = ∠B. Step 2: Similarly, ∠YAC and ∠ACB are alternate interior angles, so ∠YAC = ∠C. Step 3: The angles ∠XAB, ∠BAC, and ∠YAC together form a straight angle at A along line XY, so ∠XAB + ∠BAC + ∠YAC = 180°. Substituting from steps 1 and 2 gives ∠B + ∠A + ∠C = 180°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw XY ∥ BC through A; use alternate-interior-angle pairs to replace ∠XAB with ∠B and ∠YAC with ∠C; the three angles at A form a straight angle of 180°.

inclusivity.support: Talk through each step with a partner before writing — first name the parallel line, then name the two pairs of alternate angles.
inclusivity.challenge: Using the same parallel-line construction, derive the exterior-angle theorem: the exterior angle at C equals ∠A + ∠B.

exercise.description: Experiment with different triangles to find a relation between any two angles and the third. What data will you track and how will you organise it?

items.prompt: Using compass and ruler, construct an equilateral triangle with side length 5 cm. After constructing, measure all three sides and record your measurements. Write the two-sentence justification that explains why the third vertex C, formed by intersecting arcs of radius 5 cm from each base endpoint, is equidistant from both base endpoints.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: All three measured sides should be 5 cm (within compass-drawing tolerance). Justification: C lies on the arc centred at A with radius 5 cm, so AC = 5 cm. C also lies on the arc centred at B with radius 5 cm, so BC = 5 cm. Since AB = AC = BC = 5 cm, the triangle is equilateral.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Swing equal arcs of the same radius from both base endpoints; their intersection point is equidistant from both, making all three sides equal.

inclusivity.support: After placing C at the arc intersection, measure AC and BC separately with a ruler to confirm both equal 5 cm.
inclusivity.challenge: Explain why swinging arcs of a radius smaller than half of AB from both endpoints would prevent the arcs from intersecting at all.

items.section_title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given
items.prompt: A fence is to be built along three edges of a field. The three proposed lengths are 8 m, 15 m, and 24 m. Apply the triangle inequality to decide whether these lengths can form a triangular field. Show all three comparisons.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Check all three inequalities: (1) 8 + 15 = 23, which is less than 24 — this comparison fails. (2) 8 + 24 = 32 > 15 — passes. (3) 15 + 24 = 39 > 8 — passes. Since comparison (1) fails (23 < 24), the three lengths do not satisfy the triangle inequality and cannot form a triangle. The triangular field cannot be built with these dimensions.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check each side against the sum of the other two; 8 + 15 = 23 < 24 fails, so the triangle does not exist.

inclusivity.support: List the three sides in order and check: smallest + middle vs largest first, since that comparison is the critical one.
inclusivity.challenge: Find the smallest integer value by which the 24 m side would need to be reduced so that all three lengths can form a triangle.

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: Construct triangle ABC where the included angle at B is 65°, AB = 4 cm, and BC = 6 cm. After constructing, use the angle-sum property to calculate ∠A + ∠C, and measure ∠A and ∠C with a protractor to verify. Record both the calculated sum and the measured values.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: By the angle-sum property, ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°. Since ∠B = 65°, we get ∠A + ∠C = 180° − 65° = 115°. Measured angles will vary by student construction but ∠A + ∠C should be approximately 115° (within a degree or two of protractor tolerance).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Construct SAS (AB = 4 cm, ∠B = 65°, BC = 6 cm), then apply ∠A + ∠C = 180° − ∠B = 115° and verify by measurement.

inclusivity.support: After constructing, measure all three angles with a protractor and add them — the sum should be close to 180°.
inclusivity.challenge: Without measuring ∠A and ∠C individually, predict which will be larger by reasoning about the side lengths opposite each angle, and then verify by measurement.

items.section_title: Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles
items.prompt: Triangle DEF has an obtuse angle at E. Describe clearly, without drawing, where the foot of the altitude from vertex D will fall — on the segment EF, at a point on EF extended beyond F, or at a point on EF extended beyond E? Justify your answer using the definition of an altitude.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Since the angle at E is obtuse (greater than 90°), the perpendicular from D to the line through EF falls outside the segment EF — specifically on the extension of EF beyond E. This is because the altitude from D must be perpendicular to the line EF, and when ∠E is obtuse the interior of the triangle 'opens' on the other side, pushing the foot of the altitude past vertex E onto the extension.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the definition: the altitude is the perpendicular from the vertex to the line (not the segment) containing the opposite side; with an obtuse angle at E, the foot falls on the extension beyond E.

inclusivity.support: Sketch a rough triangle with a clearly obtuse angle at E and try to draw a perpendicular from D to the side EF — notice where the foot lands.
inclusivity.challenge: In which type of triangle do all three altitudes have their feet inside the triangle, and why? Use the angle definitions to support your answer.
